topicName: Wireless Network Attacks (WPA/WPA2/WPA3 Cracking, Rogue AP)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Wireless Network Attacks: WPA/WPA2/WPA3 Cracking and Rogue APs"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Wireless security auditing is a critical component of comprehensive penetration testing. Understanding how attackers compromise WPA, WPA2, and WPA3 protocols, as well as how they deploy Rogue Access Points, allows security professionals to better defend enterprise wireless environments."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Prerequisites and Lab Setup"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Before executing wireless attacks, ensure you have a wireless network adapter capable of packet injection and monitor mode. The Aircrack-ng suite and Hostapd-wpe are standard tools used for these assessments."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"sudo ip link set wlan0 down
sudo iwconfig wlan0 mode monitor
sudo ip link set wlan0 up"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Targeting WPA/WPA2-PSK Networks"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"WPA and WPA2 networks utilizing Pre-Shared Keys (PSK) rely on a 4-way handshake to establish a secure session. Attackers capture this handshake over-the-air and perform offline dictionary or brute-force attacks against the derived Pairwise Master Key (PMK)."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Step 1: Discover target networks and associated clients using airodump-ng."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Step 2: Force a client to re-authenticate by sending deauthentication frames, triggering a new 4-way handshake."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Step 3: Crack the captured handshake using a wordlist and aircrack-ng or hashcat."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"sudo airodump-ng --bssid 00:11:22:33:44:55 -c 6 --write target_capture wlan0mon
sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a 00:11:22:33:44:55 -c AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF wlan0mon
sudo aircrack-ng -w /path/to/wordlist.txt -b 00:11:22:33:44:55 target_capture-01.cap"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding WPA3 and SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals)"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"WPA3 was introduced to resolve the vulnerabilities of WPA2, notably replacing the vulnerable 4-way handshake with the Dragonfly handshake (SAE). SAE prevents offline dictionary attacks because each connection uses a forward-secure authenticated key exchange. However, WPA3 networks operating in transition mode (WPA2/WPA3 mixed) remain susceptible to downgrade attacks and traditional WPA2 handshaking exploits."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Deploying a Rogue Access Point (Evil Twin)"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Rogue Access Point mimics a legitimate wireless network to trick users into connecting. Once connected, attackers can perform Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks, capture credentials via captive portals, or inspect unencrypted traffic."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"sudo hostapd /etc/hostapd/hostapd.conf"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Proper mitigation includes implementing WPA3 Enterprise with Protected Management Frames (PMF), deploying Wireless Intrusion Detection Systems (WIDS) to detect unauthorized access points, and educating users on rogue network risks."}]
